## ARGUMENT

### A shotgun pleading that fails to give defendants adequate notice of the claims against them should be dismissed.

Rule 8(a)(2) requires "a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief," and Rule 10(b) requires that each claim be stated in a separate, numbered count when doing so promotes clarity. Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2), 10(b). Together, these rules ensure that a defendant can discern what is being claimed and frame a responsive pleading. This Court has long condemned complaints that defeat that purpose, calling them "shotgun pleadings." *See Cesnik v. Edgewood Baptist Church*, 88 F.3d 902, 905 (11th Cir. 1996); *Anderson v. Dist. Bd. of Trs. of Cent. Fla. Cmty. Coll.*, 77 F.3d 364, 366–67 (11th Cir. 1996).

**1. The governing standard.** In *Weiland v. Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office*, 792 F.3d 1313 (11th Cir. 2015), the Court identified four rough categories of shotgun pleadings:

- complaints in which each count adopts the allegations of all preceding counts;
- complaints filled with conclusory, vague, and immaterial facts not obviously connected to any cause of action;
- complaints that do not separate each cause of action into a different count; and
- complaints that assert multiple claims against multiple defendants without specifying which defendant is responsible for which acts or which claim applies to which defendant.

*Id.* at 1321–23; *accord Vibe Micro, Inc. v. Shabanets*, 878 F.3d 1291, 1294–95 (11th Cir. 2018). "The unifying characteristic of all types of shotgun pleadings is that they fail to one degree or another, and in one way or another, to give the defendants adequate notice of the claims against them and the grounds upon which each claim rests." *Weiland*, 792 F.3d at 1323.

**2. The harm that justifies dismissal.** The defect is not technical. When a complaint incorporates every prior count, it becomes "virtually impossible to know which allegations of fact are intended to support which claim(s) for relief." *Anderson*, 77 F.3d at 366. The defendant must then guess at the claims, and the court must sift the pleading to decide which allegations matter. *See Cramer v. Florida*, 117 F.3d 1258, 1263 (11th Cir. 1997). Shotgun pleadings also impose costs beyond the parties. They consume judicial resources, expand discovery, and burden appellate dockets. *See Jackson v. Bank of Am., N.A.*, 898 F.3d 1348, 1356–57 (11th Cir. 2018); *Vibe Micro*, 878 F.3d at 1295. The Court has described the burden as an unfair one placed on defendants and the court alike. *See Magluta v. Samples*, 256 F.3d 1282, 1284 (11th Cir. 2001) (per curiam).

**3. Dismissal is the appropriate remedy.** District courts have inherent authority to control their dockets, including by dismissing shotgun pleadings. *Weiland*, 792 F.3d at 1320; *see also Paylor v. Hartford Fire Ins. Co.*, 748 F.3d 1117, 1126 (11th Cir. 2014). This Court has repeatedly instructed that a district court confronted with such a pleading should require repleading, and has not hesitated to reverse when a court allowed a case to proceed on one. *See Jackson*, 898 F.3d at 1357–58; *Vibe Micro*, 878 F.3d at 1295–96. A court need not parse the complaint to salvage a viable claim. *Barmapov v. Amuial*, 986 F.3d 1321, 1324–25 (11th Cir. 2021) (affirming dismissal of a complaint that was a shotgun pleading and explaining that the court need not identify which allegations support which claims). Where a plaintiff has already been told of the deficiencies and has had an opportunity to cure them, dismissal with prejudice is within the court's discretion. *See Jackson*, 898 F.3d at 1357–58; *Vibe Micro*, 878 F.3d at 1295–96.

**4. Application.** [Plaintiff's] complaint falls within the *Weiland* categories. Each count incorporates by reference all preceding paragraphs, including the prior counts' legal conclusions. [Compl. ¶¶ __.] Several counts combine distinct legal theories. [Compl. ¶¶ __.] The complaint also asserts claims against [multiple defendants] collectively, without identifying which defendant is alleged to have done what. [Compl. ¶¶ __.] [Defendant] therefore cannot tell which allegations support which claims against it, or what conduct it is alleged to have committed. That is the notice failure the shotgun-pleading doctrine addresses. *Weiland*, 792 F.3d at 1323. The complaint should be dismissed.
